email.subject: URGENT: Your account has been suspended

findings.title: DMARC fail
findings.explanation: The visible From address (n0rthwind-bank.example) is not backed by a passing SPF or DKIM check. This is the strongest sign the sender is being impersonated.

findings.title: Link text hides a different destination
findings.explanation: The link says 'www.northwind-bank.example' but actually goes to '203.0.113.50'. Hovering over a link (or long-pressing on a phone) shows its real destination.

findings.title: Link points to a raw IP address
findings.explanation: Legitimate organisations link to their domain name, not a bare server address. This usually means a hastily set-up or compromised server.

findings.title: Link to a look-alike domain
findings.explanation: 'northwind-bank.example.account-verify.example' imitates 'northwind-bank.example'. Fake login pages are hosted on domains like this to collect passwords.

findings.title: Sender domain imitates northwind-bank.example
findings.explanation: The email comes from 'n0rthwind-bank.example', which is designed to look like 'northwind-bank.example' at a glance (swapped or extra characters, or the real name used as part of a different domain).

findings.title: Display name claims to be Northwind Bank
findings.explanation: The name shown is 'Northwind Bank Security', but the real address is 'security@n0rthwind-bank.example', which does not belong to northwind-bank.example. Most email apps show only the name, hiding the real address.

findings.title: Replies go to a different domain
findings.explanation: The email is from 'n0rthwind-bank.example', but pressing Reply sends your answer to 'northwind.help@freemail.example'. Scammers do this so the conversation reaches them, not the real organisation.

findings.title: SPF fail
findings.explanation: The email was sent from a server that n0rthwind-bank.example explicitly does not authorise, so the sender address is probably forged.

findings.title: Asks for passwords or personal details
findings.explanation: Real organisations never ask you to confirm a password or card details by email.

findings.title: DKIM none
findings.explanation: The email carries no digital signature from the sender's domain.

findings.title: Urgent or threatening language
findings.explanation: Creates time pressure so you act before thinking it through.

findings.title: Generic greeting
findings.explanation: Mass phishing doesn't know your name. On its own this is common in legitimate newsletters too.

findings.title: Disguised file extension
findings.explanation: 'Invoice_INV-20931.pdf.exe' pretends to be a .pdf file but is really .exe. Windows hides known extensions by default, so it shows as 'Invoice_INV-20931.pdf'.

findings.title: HTML attachment
findings.explanation: An attached web page opens locally in your browser, often as a fake sign-in form, and avoids the scanners that check links.

findings.title: DMARC none
findings.explanation: fastpay-invoices.example publishes no DMARC policy, so receiving servers have no instruction to reject forged email that claims to be from it.

findings.title: SPF softfail
findings.explanation: The email was sent from a server fastpay-invoices.example does not list as authorised. Weaker than a hard fail, but still a warning sign.

findings.title: Urgent or threatening language
findings.explanation: Creates time pressure so you act before thinking it through.

findings.title: Unusual payment request
findings.explanation: Requests for gift cards, wire transfers or changed bank details are the core of invoice and CEO fraud.

findings.title: Asks you to keep it secret
findings.explanation: Secrecy stops you checking with a colleague, which is exactly how these scams get caught.
findings.evidence: "keep this between us", "I'm in a meeting"

findings.title: Official-sounding sender using free webmail
findings.explanation: 'Sarah Mitchell (CEO)' sounds like an organisation or senior role, but the email was sent from a free freemail.example account. Organisations email from their own domain; this pattern is typical of CEO fraud.

findings.title: Urgent or threatening language
findings.explanation: Creates time pressure so you act before thinking it through.

findings.title: Link points to a raw IP address

findings.title: Link contains '@' to disguise its destination
findings.explanation: In 'https://trusted.com@evil.example', everything before the @ is ignored and the browser goes to evil.example.

findings.title: Link to a look-alike domain
findings.explanation: 'xn--nrthwind-bank-i7k.example' (displayed as 'nоrthwind-bank.example') imitates 'northwind-bank.example'. Fake login pages are hosted on domains like this to collect passwords.

findings.title: Sender domain imitates northwind-bank.example
findings.explanation: The email comes from 'xn--nrthwind-bank-i7k.example' (displayed as 'nоrthwind-bank.example'), which is designed to look like 'northwind-bank.example' at a glance (swapped or extra characters, or the real name used as part of a different domain).

findings.title: Display name claims to be Northwind Bank
findings.explanation: The name shown is 'Northwind Bank', but the real address is 'alerts@xn--nrthwind-bank-i7k.example', which does not belong to northwind-bank.example. Most email apps show only the name, hiding the real address.

findings.title: Asks for passwords or personal details
findings.explanation: Real organisations never ask you to confirm a password or card details by email.

findings.title: Sender domain uses international characters
findings.explanation: The domain 'xn--nrthwind-bank-i7k.example' (displayed as 'nоrthwind-bank.example') is written in punycode (xn--), meaning it contains non-Latin characters that can look identical to normal letters.
